subject: technology
unit_title: AI, Machine Learning Literacy, and Evaluation
essential_question: How do we tell whether a model is good, and good for whom?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Data and Analysis
project_brief: Evaluate a supplied model or AI output against metrics, baselines, bias analysis, and disclosure requirements. This is the grade 11 culminating project for "AI, Machine Learning Literacy, and Evaluation" (ma-g11-technology-u05, unit 5), built around supervised learning concepts, training data and representativeness, evaluation metrics and baselines, bias fairness and harm analysis, and interpretability and limitations. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to supervised learning concepts, training data and representativeness, evaluation metrics and baselines, and bias fairness and harm analysis, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: supervised learning concepts, training data and representativeness, evaluation metrics and baselines, bias fairness and harm analysis, interpretability and limitations, and responsible and disclosed AI use.
Meet the performance task as written: Evaluate a supplied model or AI output against metrics, baselines, bias analysis, and disclosure requirements.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to supervised learning concepts, training data and representativeness, evaluation metrics and baselines, and bias fairness and harm analysis, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to supervised learning concepts or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering supervised learning concepts in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to training data and representativeness, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
